sentences.text: Albertonectes vanderveldei is recognized as the longest known elasmosaurid, reaching a total length of 11.2 meters, with seven meters of that span dedicated to its neck.
This neck was supported by 76 cervical vertebrae, a count that holds the record for the greatest number of neck bones in any vertebrate.
The animal was further distinguished by a series of longitudinal lateral ridges located near the body of each cervical vertebra.
Its forelimb structure included a relatively thin humerus.
Estimates of its total body mass vary, with a 2024 study suggesting around 4.8 metric tons and a 2026 study providing a lower estimate of 3.1 metric tons for an individual of the same length.
Albertonectes possesses the highest number of cervical vertebrae of any known vertebrate, totaling 76 bones.
The holotype specimen preserves 97 visible gastroliths, or stomach stones, with the largest individual weighing an estimated 1.13 kilograms and measuring up to 13.5 centimeters in diameter.
Evidence of scavenging is preserved on the left coracoid, which bears grooves made by the shark Squalicorax.
The genus Albertonectes was described by Kubo and colleagues in 2012 from a skeleton found near Lethbridge, Alberta, in 2007.
The holotype was found accidentally by an excavator working for Korite International Ltd. during ammolite mining in Lethbridge, southern Alberta, Canada.
The fossil was found in the Bearpaw Formation, dating from the late Campanian to early Maastrichtian.
Grooves on the left coracoid indicate the animal was scavenged by the shark Squalicorax after death, a conclusion supported by tooth marks, shark scales, and related bone disturbances.
Analysis of the shape of the gastroliths suggests many were collected near a beach, and researchers hypothesize that plesiosaurs specifically selected hard chert stones for their durability.
The holotype is identified as a mature individual based on fused neural spines and partial fusion of the femur head.
Albertonectes belongs to the family Elasmosauridae and is classified within the subfamily Elasmosaurinae.
In 2016, Rodrigo A. Otero established the subfamily Styxosaurinae to include Albertonectes and three other genera, but in 2020, this subfamily was formally synonymized with Elasmosaurinae.
Albertonectes lived in North America during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 73.5 million years ago, within a broader timeframe between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
The original authors noted that assigning Albertonectes to Elasmosauridae was problematic without a skull, as skulls provide key diagnostic features.
